Gallery founder Marianne Rosenberg describes Slobodkina as someone who “defied any particular descriptive art label and was a free spirit focused on her work and not on the expectations of others.” The recent resurgence of interest, Ross says, ties into a wider reevaluation of women artists’ practices. “Contemporary audiences seem more receptive to artists whose careers do not resolve into a single movement, medium, or signature style,” she said. “The very multiplicity that may once have made Slobodkina difficult to categorize makes her feel remarkably current.”

title: Zaha Hadid Foundation to open refurbished London building as public arts space.
summary: In the 10th anniversary year of Zaha Hadid 's death, the Zaha Hadid Foundation is reopening its former headquarters at 10 Bowling Green Lane in London as a public cultural space for architecture, design, and related arts. A press and private view is scheduled for October 29th ahead of a public opening on November 3rd. The Victorian schoolhouse, built in the early 1870s, served as Hadid's practice for more than 30 years. The foundation’s refurbishment, led by Katherine Nolan and Alex Butterworth of London-based Studio KA, restores original features including a fireplace and doorways while preserving details Hadid herself introduced, such as Z-shaped door pulls and shard-like flooring insets. The reconfigured ground floor will house galleries, a learning space, a lecture hall, and collection displays, alongside Zaha Hadid Design, which features furniture and objects by Hadid and her studio. The building’s debut exhibition, “Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance,” curated by Catherine Howe and Libby Sellers, is the Foundation's first collection-based show, tracing how Hadid’s architectural language extended into stage and set design for dance, opera, and pop music, with projects spanning her 1989 collaboration with choreographer Rosemary Butcher to her 2014 staging of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Così fan tutte . A second gallery will debut “The Rebar Beneath,” an 11-minute video commission by multidisciplinary artist LionHeart developed through research in Hadid's archive, while illustrator Mona Chalabi has created a timeline visualization of Hadid’s life and work for the Foundation’s foyer. That will be projected onto a textile referencing an Issey Miyake coat from Hadid’s own wardrobe, now held in the collection. The reopening will be marked by “89° of Zaha Hadid,” a two-day symposium on October 30th and 31st—the latter being Hadid's birthday—organized with the Architectural Association and the Serpentine , which built her first completed structure, a temporary pavilion, in 2000. “It was Zaha's wish for the Foundation to preserve her legacy while carrying her ideas forward,” said Rana Hadid, chair of the Foundation's trustees, in a statement, calling the archive “a profound record of her work, imagination and intellectual life.” The relaunch follows a June court ruling that ended the Foundation's royalty agreement with Hadid's former practice, now operating simply as ZHA, and comes under Foundation director Aric Chen, who since 2025 has pushed to open Hadid's archive, once described by her AA tutor Rem Koolhaas as belonging to “a planet in her own orbit,” to wider public view.

title: 10 Japanese Women Artists You Should Know
summary: In the 20th century, Japan was scarred by war and marked by anxiety and alienation. Throughout the nation’s rapid industrialization and modernization, the radical women artists of the post-war period created work that demonstrated their conviction that art could liberate them and change society. They included some of the most important artists in the world, such as Yoko Ono , Yayoi Kusama , and Ruth Asawa . Against this backdrop, Mudam Luxembourg’s landmark exhibition “Kaihō: Japanese Women Artists after 1945” brings together more than 120 works by 39 of these artists. The accompanying catalogue, published by Phaidon in English, goes even deeper to reassess the ways these artists, many of whose work has never been seen outside Japan, contributed to major art movements. Japanese women’s political agency and sexual autonomy came relatively late, compared to Western countries. They voted for the first time in 1946. Birth control pills were only legalized in Japan in 1999. Despite the setbacks, several works in “Kaihō” question the reproductive and caregiving roles traditionally assigned to women. In a video called Portrait (1998), artists Yoshiko Shimada and BuBu de la Madeleine pose as a U.S. Occupation soldier and a sex worker serving the Occupation forces, respectively, using drag as a tool to critique colonial history. Mudam’s curatorial team, led by Florence Ostende and assisted by Yurika Imaseki and Anaël Daoud, have been mindful of including lesser-known diaspora artists such as painter Tomie Ohtake , who migrated to São Paulo in 1936, forging a successful career there. Also included is the second-generation Okinawan Japanese artist from Hawaii, Toshiko Takaezu , whose ceramic “Moons” sit quietly in the corner of the final room, evoking “an elemental continuum of sky, volcanic earth, and Pacific Ocean,” according to the gallery caption. “You could see this show as a manifesto of how we should be looking for global modernism,” Ostende told Artsy. “All sense of national borders and limitations were challenged. These artists did not necessarily concede to Japan’s national identity. They really exploded the boundaries.” Here are 10 post-war Japanese women artists you need to know. Taeko Tomiyama B. 1921, Kobe, Japan. D. 2021, Tokyo. Taeko Tomiyama firmly believed that art could transform society. Having spent her childhood in Japanese-occupied Manchuria, she returned to her own country in the final years of the war. Her early lithographic works documented unemployed coal miners in the 1950s during Japan’s energy revolution. She became involved in the Japan–Korea solidarity movement in the ’70s and ’80s, supporting Korean political prisoners. The artist also made a series of lithographs in protest of the violent suppression of Gwangju’s pro-democracy movement in May 1980, some of which are displayed in the gallery. A standout work in the Mudam show is Tomiyama’s exquisitely detailed, harrowing painting, The Night of the Festival of Galungan (1986). Part of her “Memory of the Sea” series, it addresses the subject of Korean “comfort women” forced to serve the Japanese military. The dark oil painting depicts the world of the dead, a throng of skeletons on one side, garishly painted masks on the other. Lower down, women’s splayed legs are served up on a plate ceremoniously. They are all coming to haunt the terrified Japanese soldiers at the bottom of the painting. Saori Akutagawa B. 1924, Toyohashi, Japan. D. 1966, Tokyo. Saori Akutagawa originally trained as a singer, but when her husband, a composer whom she met at Tokyo College of Music, complained about her singing, she turned to “the silent art of painting.” By the 1950s, she had found the outlet she needed to express “something burning inside.” Her dye-on-cloth pieces Woman (B) and Woman (I) (both 1955) open the Mudam show, immediately pulling in viewers with their bold, vivid colors. Akutagawa once said she wanted to “rekindle the laughter of ancient deities in the modern world.” Woman A, The Hawk and Princess Kasuga (1955), appears to be an abstracted portrait of the artist herself, its angular shapes bursting with explosive energy. Akutagawa would later divorce her husband. After briefly studying in L.A., she moved to New York in the 1960s. Gaining momentum in abstraction, she exhibited alongside Kusama and Yuki Katsura , using her maiden name, Yamada. Sadly, she passed away soon after at the age of 42. Takako Saito B. 1929, Sabae, Japan. D. 2025, Düsseldorf. Grinder Chess, circa 1964 Takako Saito Doyle Untitled (Handstamped Drawing), 1985 Takako Saito OSMOS After moving to New York in the early ’60s, the self-taught artist and former teacher Takako Saito became part of the Fluxus movement, joining other Japanese women artists, such as Ono, Shigeko Kubota , and Mieko Shiomi . Fluxus suited her carefree spirit and disdain for convention. Her playful works, such as Sound Chess (1964), a large chess set with pieces only distinguishable by the sound they make, are displayed in the Mudam’s expansive foyer, alongside Ono’s Mend Piece (1966/2026) and Refugee Boat (1960/2026). In the interactive series of carved wooden heads, Spielkopf (1966–87), the viewer can drop a small bead into a sculpted head, which rolls down inside it, then pops back out unexpectedly from a different hole each time. In another gallery, Saito’s Freedom Portraitspiel No. 4 ( 1992), a sculpture made of pinecones, stones, and wooden squares, arranged whimsically in a shiny metal box, is on view. Large ears stick out on each side, while small black-and-white cubes, reminiscent of her Sound Chess , are draped along the bottom as if a piece of jewelry. Kimiyo Mishima B. 1932, Osaka. D. 2024, Osaka. Kimiyo Mishima ’s delicate trompe l’oeil sculptures take up a large part of one of the galleries. Dissatisfied with the collages she had been making using collected newspaper clippings, she began transforming them into printed or painted ceramics. These works replicated everyday objects or items of trash in the ’70s, some expanding in scale in the ’80s, as in her Coca-Cola Box (1986). “To me, the most interesting thing about ceramics was that it breaks,” Mishima said. The artist was living through Japan’s rapid economic growth and emerging information society, whose anxieties around endless news cycles find an echo today in the rise of AI. “All information instantly becomes trash as soon as it is consumed,” reads a quote next to the artwork. Mishima’s childhood was shaped by war. Seeing her hometown in Osaka destroyed after emerging from an air raid shelter one day had a lasting impact. Although her husband, Shigeji Mishima, was part of the avant-garde group Gutai , Mishima chose to work independently, forging her own path to self-expression. Atsuko Tanaka B. 1932, Osaka. D. 2005, Nara, Japan. Work (TO1018), 1970 Atsuko Tanaka Whitestone Gallery Two large-scale paintings by Atsuko Tanaka dominate the gallery dedicated to new forms of abstraction. Thick with clashing colors and drizzles of paints over abstract circles, they are delightfully barmy and reflect her interest in networks, flows, and circularity. The works brim with energy and possibility. Her Work (Bell ) (1955), which the artist would call “her invisible painting,” consists of 20 electric alarm bells connected by electrical wiring and cords. At Mudam, this has been installed across the carpeted floor in front of her colorful paintings. When the push-button switch attached to the work is activated by a visitor, a loud sound is emitted, forcing us to pay attention and really “see” her work, perhaps for the first time. Celebrated for her conceptual and performance works, including the 1956 Denkifuku (Electric Dress) in which she draped her body in hundreds of fluorescent light bulbs, Tanaka was a core member of the Gutai Association. Round of Sand (1968), a film shot on a beach of Awaji Island and displayed in a gallery dedicated to the environment, we see Tanaka drawing concentric circles into the sand. She carries on drawing despite incoming waves repeatedly erasing her work. The work is emblematic of Gutai’s concerns with the dissolution of fixed form and the body’s intervention in material. Shigeko Kubota B. 1937, Niigata, Japan. D. 2015, New York. Chess II, 1975 Shigeko Kubota Galerie Hubert Winter Shigeko Kubota was overshadowed by her more famous artist husband, Nam June Paik , but she was a pioneer of video art in her own right. In 1964, she left Japan for New York, having been disappointed by the reception of her immersive solo show in Tokyo. She joined the Fluxus group and began making video installations, incorporating mirrors and water to convey her concept of “liquid reality.” In Niagara Falls (1985–87), CRT monitors, mirrors, and other reflective surfaces are arranged in a violent cascade, against which water flows into a tank filled with shards of broken glass. The work also includes amplified sounds of waterfalls, giving the installation a dangerous feeling, and references the precarity of nature’s commodification into a tourist destination. Later in life, Kubota made work about her experience of caring for Paik, following his stroke in 1996. Bringing the ups and downs of life into art was the very essence of Fluxus. Sayako Kishimoto B. 1939, Nagoya, Japan. D. 1988, Nagoya. Instead of signing her paintings with her name, Sayako Kishimoto drew an inverted triangle to denote her fervent belief that what is at the bottom of society should be placed at the top. Her magnificent, 19-meter-long scroll, 21c. Erotica Flying Machines – A Trip to the Galaxy (1983), originally a backdrop for her own live performances, has been reproduced for this exhibition. It depicts an elaborate cosmic allegory, a world inhabited by grasshoppers and butterflies, a place of love and freedom. In the series of paintings “Erotical Girls” (1983), names of women like Pansy or Dogtooth Violet are incorporated into the titles. These women are painted in bright colors, their faces heavily made up: kitsch, unnatural, and grotesque. A nearby TV monitor shows a televised address as part of her 1983 campaign for the House of Councilors. In the video, Kishimoto asks for voter support, representing Zatsuminto (Miscellaneous People’s Party), a minority Japanese political party founded and led by LGBTQ+ and social activist Takeshi “Ken” Togo. “The suppression of gay people equals the suppression of freedom of all people,” she says. Kishimoto briefly joined the Neo-Dada Organizers as the only female member of the group in 1960, while she was still a student at Tama Art University. She moved back to her hometown of Nagoya when she was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 40. The cancer would take her life nine years later. Tāri Itō B. 1951, Tokyo. D. 2021, Tokyo. Like Kishimoto, Tāri Itō was a pioneering performance artist and social activist, her work exploring embodied resistance and questioning normative gender identity. In her performance, Self-Portrait (1996), latex rubber becomes Itō’s second skin, as she blows air through a pipe to expand different areas of her body, while asking directly to the camera, “Who are you?” She answers the question herself: “I am not married; I have no child.” Finally, she reveals that she is a lesbian. Itō is quoted in the exhibition catalogue saying that her performances, like Me Being Me (1996), gave her “great joy.” She built networks of like-minded artists and activists in Japan, Europe, East and Southeast Asia, eventually founding the Women’s Art Network (WAN, 1994–2008) back in Japan. The triple disaster of the earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear power meltdown on March 11, 2011, led Itō to make one of her final performance works, I guess it’s better that radiation doesn’t have color …Sigh (2011), in which she used LED lights and fluorescent-painted latex and onions to make visible the fear of radiation. Despite the degenerative neurological illness she developed in her later years, she still joined demonstrations and participated in group exhibitions, the last of which was in 2019. Mao Ishikawa B. 1953, Okinawa, Japan. Lives and works in Okinawa. Setting out to photograph American soldiers in her hometown Okinawa’s military bases, Mao Ishikawa was soon drawn to the women working in bars in Japan’s Koza City and Kin Town, catering to the men’s needs. She wanted to capture the Okinawan women who lived “freely and uninhibitedly,” defying social contempt. Ishikawa’s early work, Red Flowers (Akabanaa) (1975–77), some of which are displayed in the exhibition, shows these women at ease in Ishikawa’s gaze, sometimes looking straight back at the lens. In a transitional section of the gallery, where the postcard-size portraits of all 39 artists are displayed, we see Ishikawa’s black-and-white self-portrait, taken after surviving cancer in 2001–02. In this photo, scars on her body are painfully visible. Her lifelong inquiry into what it means to be an Okinawan, as distinct and separate from the imposed national identity, led to her series “Here’s What the Japanese Flag Means to Me” (1993–2011), made in collaboration with the Ainu people, Burakumin, Taiwanese, and Korean residents in Japan. In her ongoing, large-scale photographic project, The Great Ryukyu Photo Scroll (2014–present), her friends and family reenact scenes from Okinawa’s history. Nobuho Nagasawa B. 1959, Tokyo. Lives and works in New York. Utsusemi, 2018 Nobuho Nagasawa Japan Society Benefit Auction Informed by her nomadic, multicultural upbringing, Nobuho Nagasawa ’s work challenges a nationalist framing of identity. The artist is known for her participatory site-responsive installations that could be climbed over and even inhabited. Nagasawa studied art, critical theory, and music in Berlin and California, spending time in Tokoname, Japan, where she studied under the ceramist Ryoji Koie , and eventually settling in New York. The artist sees ecology as inseparable from art. Her later works adapt LED technology and fiber-optic cables. In her 2013 TED Talk, Nagasawa said, “I combine the natural world—rain, wind, waves, and bird songs with human sounds, like heartbeat and voices, and I transform them into light.” In 2023, her early earthworks Noyaki (1984) and Navel of the Earth (1985) were included in the Mori Art Museum’s 20th-anniversary exhibition, “Our Ecology: Toward a Planetary Living.” In a grainy video on view in the Mudam show, the artist is shown creating one of her earthworks with a group of Tokoname residents—laughing, shouting, and being herself.

title: 5 Standout Shows to See at Small Galleries This October
summary: Chase, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery In this monthly roundup, we spotlight five stellar exhibitions at small and rising galleries. Chuma Adam and Siyabonga Fani “ Catching ” 99 Loop Gallery , Cape Town Through Oct. 24 Blackness as self-actualization: Umkhondo (A Trail/Mark), 2026 Chuma Adam 99 Loop Gallery umlambo, 2026 Siyabonga Fani 99 Loop Gallery This two-person show brings together the work of South African artists Chuma Adam and Siyabonga Fani in a meditation on materials and their connections to memory. Rising artist Chuma Adam presents monochrome paintings in acrylic on umbhaco cotton, a textile traditionally used to make Xhosa ceremonial garments in South Africa. Her painting process is intensive and physically demanding, with individual, repetitive brushstrokes coalescing into a sea of gestures. Adam was born in 2001 and is based in Johannesburg. She earned an honors degree in fine arts from the University of the Witwatersrand in 2024 and was shortlisted for the Wits Young Artist Award in 2022 and 2023. Her broader practice encompasses painting, printmaking, textiles, sculpture, and drawing, exploring themes of Blackness, identity, and visibility. 99 Loop Gallery places Adam’s works in a compelling dialogue with Siyabonga Fani ’s evocative ceramic vessels. Fani has worked with clay since the 1990s, choosing recycled terra-cotta, a material that carries its own histories. He builds his works freehand, coiling the clay intuitively to create vessels that are highly glossy and marked by organic cracks and rivulets. Fani’s father was a self-taught artist, and Fani draws on paternal inheritance in his process. Fani was born in 1981 in Gugulethu, Cape Town, and currently works in Woodstock, Cape Town. His interest in ceramics emerged while he was a student at the College of Cape Town, and he founded Siyabonga Ceramics in 2013. His works were exhibited at the Investec Cape Town Art Fair, Latitudes Art Fair, and Homo Faber in Venice in 2024, and he had his first solo show, “Ndim Lo [This Is Me],” at Art Formes in Cape Town in 2025. Matija Bobičić “ The Kingdom ” Moosey , Norwich, England Through Oct. 31 The Green Hero, 2026 Matija Bobicic Moosey The Werewolf Queen, 2026 Matija Bobicic Moosey Matija Bobičić ’s acrylic-on-canvas paintings look like what might result if Jean-Michel Basquiat tried his hand at painting Biblically accurate angels. The Slovenian artist’s chimerical figures draw from science fiction, pop culture, and Balkan folklore: Baseball-capped bobbleheads, skulls, and dinosaurs all populate the creatures’ wings. In this new exhibition, Bobičić presents figures that, according to the artist, emerge from “the archetypes of Frankenstein’s monster and the cyborg, the context of the early 1990s, and the challenges of the present moment.” In The Green Hero (2026), for example, a Ninja Turtle is made up of clown-like faces and totemic masks. Bobičić has also noted his fascination with Warhammer 40,000 , a tabletop game and fictional universe whose characters inspire his figures. The artist fuses these techno-futuristic aesthetics with symbols from Balkan folklore. The artist was born in 1987 in Maribor, Slovenia, where he lives and works. He graduated from the University of Maribor with a degree in art education in 2016. Bobičić has shown with galleries including Marvin Gardens in New York (2018, 2021), Breach Gallery in Miami (2022), Allouche Gallery in Los Angeles (2022), and Alchemy Gallery in New York (2023). He also presented a solo exhibition, “Perfect Organisms,” at the Maribor Art Gallery in Slovenia, and his work has since entered the museum’s collection. Hisham Sharif “ Allusive Veil ” Ayyam Gallery , Dubai Through Oct. 30 Behind the Window, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery Red Room with a Rothko, 2026 Hisham Sharif Ayyam Gallery Hisham Sharif makes his U.A.E. solo debut with “ Allusive Veil ,” an exhibition of alluring and ambiguous paintings rooted in heritage and mythology. Sharif’s technique draws on French painters, particularly Bonnard and Vuillard , and their rhythmic, almost psychedelic interiors. Yet his style is firmly contemporary, his scenes pushed to near abstraction. In the painting Behind the Window (2026), for example, the curtained plane of a window gives way to streaking horizontal lines, creating a sense of disorientation. The show also marks Sharif’s first significant use of color, a departure from the monochrome work for which he was previously known. Born in 1993 in Bahrain, Sharif is the son of artist Abdul Rahim Sharif , who trained in Paris in the 1970s. His past exhibitions include “Frightening the Dark,” his first solo show, in 2017 at the Bahrain Arts Society, and “Sharif & Sharif” in 2022 at the Bahrain Art Centre. He won the Al Dana Award at the 50th Bahrain Annual Fine Arts Exhibition and received a Recognition Award for Outstanding Work at the 45th edition. His work is in the permanent collection of the Bahrain National Museum. Granite Calimpong “ Under the Bank, Up a Narrow Valley ” Traver Gallery , Seattle Through Oct. 31 MURKY, 2026 Granite Calimpong Traver Gallery SWEET SMELLS OF HERE, 2026 Granite Calimpong Traver Gallery Seattle-based sculptor Granite Calimpong explores his relationship with the rugged California coast where he grew up and the Pacific Northwest, where he has lived for nearly two decades, through a series of odd, biomorphic, and delightful ceramic and glass works. In these pieces, Calimpong conjures iridescent surfaces, crusty formations, and mushroom-like protrusions. Made with both glass and ceramics, the works are caught in a state of material flux between earthen depth and shiny translucence, a hint at the duality of the natural world today, where ecological crisis lives alongside the splendor and magic of adaptation. Calimpong, born in 1982, is the son of California potter Conrad Calimpong. He earned a degree in interdisciplinary computing in the arts from the University of California, San Diego, where he was introduced to glass, and later an MFA in sculpture from the University of Washington in 2019. He has held residencies at the Pittsburgh Glass Center (2013) and North Lands Creative Glass in Scotland (2016), and has had recent solo shows at Traver Gallery (2023) and JamFactory in Adelaide, Australia (2023). He is also a teacher who has led workshops at Pilchuck Glass School, Penland School of Craft, and Haystack Mountain School of Crafts. Zoe Hawk “ Lost Girls ” Visions West Contemporary , Denver Oct. 9–Nov. 21 Search Party, 2026 Zoe Hawk Visions West Contemporary Portal, 2025 Zoe Hawk Visions West Contemporary Zoe Hawk paints candy-colored visions of girlhood—campfire scenes, dances, walks in the woods—but these visions are more sinister than saccharine. In Search Party (2026), for example, a group of doll-like girls walks through the snowy woods, calling out for a lost girl as a fox stalks the trees between them. In another work, The Well (2026), moody girls in knee-high socks and Mary Janes throw rocks into a stone well. These disquieting paintings suggest dark feminine rituals. They are reminiscent of the Showtime series Yellowjackets , in which a girls’ soccer team gets stranded in the woods and begins to turn on each other. Born in 1982 in St. Louis, Hawk is now based in Columbia, Missouri. She earned a BFA in studio art from Missouri State University and an MFA in painting from the University of Iowa. She has attended residencies in Ireland, Norway, Belgium, and Qatar, and at the Women’s Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York. Her works have been included in exhibitions such as “From Pangs to Pangolins,” curated by Trenton Doyle Hancock , at Shulamit Nazarian in Los Angeles in 2018. She had a solo show, “Dreaming as the Summers Die,” at Glass Rice in San Francisco that same year, and her work was featured in Zara’s Women in Art clothing collection in 2019.

title: Annie Leibovitz photographs OpenAI's Sam Altman in Caspar David Friedrich-inspired portrait for Vanity Fair.
summary: Annie Leibovitz has photographed OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for the cover of 2026 “New Establishment” issue of Vanity Fair, accompanying a two-part interview with the magazine. The cover portrait depicts Altman from behind, hands on hips, surveying a foggy coastline from a cliff's edge. The photograph is accompanied by a line of text reading, “Sam Altman sees the future—are we in it?” The composition appears to be a restaging of German Romantic artist Caspar David Friedrich 's iconic 1818 painting Wanderer above the Sea of Fog , now held in the collection of the Hamburger Kunsthalle. The painting is considered a definitive example of the “Rückenfigur,” an artistic device showing a figure turned away in order to invite viewers to imagine themselves in the painting. Friedrich's wanderer, shown in a green overcoat, gazing out over a misty mountain landscape, has often been interpreted as contemplation of the sublime, the fog a symbol of the unknown future. In Leibovitz's interpretation, Friedrich's vision of the Elbe Sandstone cliffs in Bohemia is replaced by Bay Area bluffs, and Altman stands in as the solitary man positioned at the edge of a cliff. While Friedrich’s figure contemplated nature’s connection to divinity, Altman, it might be inferred, contemplates the future of artificial intelligence. The reference offers an uneasy inversion, with Friedrich’s figure enthralled by nature, and Altman, the artificial and technological. Altman’s cover story leads Vanity Fair’ s revived “New Establishment” list, with the tech CEO addressing AI safety lapses, government regulation, and his rivalry with Elon Musk in an interview. This is far from the first time Leibovitz has looked to art history for inspiration, linking her subjects to famed precedents for beauty, power, or interiority. In 2002, she photographed actress Salma Hayek as Frida Kahlo for Vogue , drawing on Kahlo's own self-portraiture. For a 2013 Vogue shoot, she restaged eight famous paintings using actress Jessica Chastain as her model. The cover pictured Chastain as Frederic Leighton 's Flaming June, with reimaginings of works by Vincent van Gogh , René Magritte , Félix Vallotton , and Julia Margaret Cameron accompanying the feature story. More recently, Leibovitz's August 2025 Vogue cover story styled Anne Hathaway as John Singer Sargent 's Madame X .

title: JW Anderson to host a London pop-up show with artist Cerith Wyn Evans during Frieze Week 2026.
summary: JW Anderson flagship store in Pimlico, London. The exhibition centers on a new series of 30 wind chimes that Cerith Wyn Evans developed specifically for the brand, shown alongside selected works by the artist courtesy of White Cube , his representing gallery. The show, which also brings together designers, makers, and long-standing collaborators from Anderson's creative world, is open to the public from October 15th through 20th, coinciding with Frieze London. Other works on view include ceramics by Akiko Hirai , paintings by Mary Stephenson , and sculptures by Shawanda Corbett . “A Composition” is presented in partnership with American Express, and Amex Platinum Cardmembers will receive a dedicated preview day on October 14th, ahead of the public opening. They will also receive a complimentary gift from JW Anderson and an exclusive limited-edition work on paper and bookmark with purchase. The exhibition extends Anderson's long-running involvement in the art world as both collector and curator. His personal collection includes ceramic works by artists Lucie Rie , Jennifer Lee , and Sara Flynn , as well as powerhouses of the 1980s including Peter Hujar and David Wojnarowicz . He has curated exhibitions for the Hepworth Wakefield, the Holburne Museum, and London's Thomas Dane Gallery, and in 2023 organized the group show “ On Foot ” at Offer Waterman , also in London. Anderson has also made art collaboration central to his design work. For his Dior Cruise 2027 collection, shown at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , he worked with Ed Ruscha on a series of Dior Homme button-down shirts referencing the artist's signature lettering and shadowing. For his brand, JW Anderson, he has previously partnered with the Tom of Finland Foundation and the estate of David Wojnarowicz . “A Composition” follows other recent exhibitions at the JW Anderson store, which has developed into something of a gallery space in its own right for the brand.

title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani doubles individual artist grants in New York City to $10,000.
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice Julie Su, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs (DCLA) Commissioner Diya Vij have announced that the city will increase its grants for individual artists and small nonprofits from $5,000 to $10,000, the first such increase in nearly 20 years. Grants, which are distributed through partners in each borough, are open to artists, collectives, and small nonprofits working across film, dance, writing, painting, and other disciplines. Applications are now open in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Manhattan, and Queens. Staten Island's cycle opens in November. Alongside the increase, DCLA's Materials for the Arts program will also launch a monthly “shopping day” for grantees to access free art supplies. “Artists are working New Yorkers with the same costs as everyone else. But while rent, grocery bills, and child care costs have skyrocketed in New York City, the funding artists rely on has stayed flat,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Doubling these grants is a critical step towards making sure that the painters, musicians, filmmakers, and other artists who bring life to this city can afford to call it home.” Vij, who said she spent the past six months in town halls with working artists across the five boroughs, called the increase “our first step to deeper, more meaningful support.” Mamdani also relayed the news in a more informal Instagram announcement . In the clip, he is filmed painting at an easel across from Vij, saying, “Artists are forced to make hard choices when it comes to living in this city and getting paid. There's never been a better time to apply.” According to Hyperallergic , the news follows a $323.8 million allocation for DCLA in the city's Fiscal Year 2027 budget. It marks the highest-ever yearly appropriation for the agency, which ensures public funding to supports cultural organizations throughout New York City. A January report from the Center for an Urban Future noted that the city's resident artist population has fallen 4.4 percent since 2019, its first measurable decline in decades. The increase extends a pattern of arts investment under Mamdani , who in July announced a Groundswell Community Mural Project commissioning 12 artist-led, community-painted murals across the five boroughs for the FIFA World Cup 2026 . Mamdani has separately partnered with the Met Opera and the Theatre Development Fund to expand free and low-cost access to performances for New York residents and students.

title: Hirshhorn Sculpture Garden to reopen in October 2026 following Hiroshi Sugimoto redesign.
summary: The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden 's Sculpture Garden in Washington, DC, will reopen on October 31st following a reimagining of the landscape by Japanese artist and architect Hiroshi Sugimoto . The project marks the most significant rethinking of the garden since American modernist architect Gordon Bunshaft conceived the Hirshhorn's distinctive cylindrical museum and sunken sculpture garden more than half a century ago. The garden first opened to the public in 1974. In 1981, landscape architect Lester Collins added additional lawns, trees, ramps, and shaded outdoor spaces. Sugimoto's intervention preserves the essential character of Bunshaft's modernist campus while creating a more open, varied, and flexible setting for the museum's collection of modern and contemporary sculpture. Central to the design is a series of monumental, stacked stone walls that divide the landscape into a sequence of distinct but interconnected spaces, including the East and Central Gardens and West Lawn. The stone offers an elemental counterpoint to Bunshaft's concrete architecture and a restrained backdrop for sculpture spanning more than a century. The redesigned garden will allow the Hirshhorn to display 50 percent more artworks outdoors. Some 24 major sculptures from Joseph H. Hirshhorn's Foundational Gift will return to view, including works by Auguste Rodin , Henri Matisse , Henry Moore , Alberto Giacometti , and Barbara Hepworth , presented in dialogue with living artists and new commissions rather than organized as a chronological survey. A wider “front door” will create at-grade sightlines into the garden from the National Mall, while five points of entry, new east and west overlooks, twice as many accessible entrances, and expanded shade and seating will make the previously secluded space more porous. An underground passageway will reconnect the garden directly to the museum, establishing a physical route between the indoor galleries, Sugimoto's landscape, and the Mall. According to the Washington Post , the overhaul also includes a revamped reflecting pool. and A rotating exhibition program will also launch with a spotlight on large aluminum figures by Yoshitomo Nara . Sugimoto's design extends his longstanding relationship with the Hirshhorn, which was the first museum to present a major retrospective of his work and, in 2018, invited him to reimagine its lobby.

title: Lee Krasner Steps Out From Pollock’s Shadow
summary: In 1957, Lee Krasner moved her painting tools and set up her studio in the barn on the property of her home in Springs, New York, a hamlet in eastern Long Island. The barn—a single-light-filled space measuring roughly 20 by 20 feet—had previously been the studio of her late husband, Jackson Pollock . But from 1957 until Krasner’s death in 1984, the barn was her domain, and there she took full advantage of the space and freedom finally afforded her, producing the most brilliant works of her career. A dazzling new exhibition, “ Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous ” at the Metropolitan Museum of Art , brings together the works of husband and wife, tracing the trajectory of their careers. The show begins with Krasner, opening with a series of abstract collage paintings from the mid-1950s made from cut-up fragments of her old canvases and drawings. It concludes with Krasner, too, closing with Past Continuous (1976), a monumental collage Krasner made from her own Cubist -inspired drawings from the 1930s from which the show takes its name. Pollock’s breathtaking drip paintings appear in the middle like a storm, a force of nature that tore through Krasner’s life. In his lifetime, Pollock had become synonymous with the barn. There, he had flung, dripped, and poured paint onto canvases unrolled across its floors. In 1949, Life magazine immortalized Pollock and his studio with a profile entitled “Is He the Greatest Living Painter in the United States?” The editorial featured photographer Martha Holmes’s now-iconic images of Pollock at work, dripping paint from a brush with a cigarette dangling from his lips. Pollock and Krasner had moved to Springs from New York City in 1945, using a loan from gallerist and collector Peggy Guggenheim for the down payment on a two-story home. They had come to the bucolic seaside town seeking an escape from the distractions and demands of city life so they could focus on their work. Pollock first worked in an upstairs bedroom and Krasner in the cramped kitchen. Later, Pollock moved his studio into the property’s barn, and Krasner took the upstairs bedroom he had vacated. In August 1956, Pollock crashed his car on the side of the road after a night of heavy drinking, killing himself and his passenger, Edith Metzger, a friend of his mistress, Ruth Kligman. Kligman, who was also in the car, survived. Krasner, who had been traveling in Europe at the time of the crash, returned immediately to plan his funeral. Slowly, in the months that followed, she returned to her practice, eventually moving her tools into the barn, close to a year after his death. For many years, the barn had smelled of the kerosene used to heat a stove, but Pollock had winterized it in 1953, insulating the walls and covering the floor with Masonite squares left over from a printing job by his brother, Sanford. When Krasner entered the studio in 1957, she walked on tiles that hid Pollock’s paint splatters covering the wood floor beneath. Often, stories of Krasner’s life seem to end with Pollock’s death, but in reality, she was just embarking on the most fruitful years of her artistic career. Krasner, a rising star She was born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn in 1908, the fourth of six children in a working-class, Orthodox Jewish household where English, Russian, and Yiddish mingled. Krasner rebelled early and leaned into art. She studied at the Woman’s Art School of Cooper Union, the National Academy of Design (which suspended her for entering a basement off-limits to women), and City College, before she enrolled in 1937 at the Hans Hofmann School of Fine Arts. There, as The Met’s exhibition catalogue notes, she “imbibed the tenets of Cubism and came to revere Henri Matisse .” In late 1941, the painter John Graham invited her to show in “American and French Paintings” at McMillen Inc. Krasner, who had cultivated friendships with many in the New York art world, knew every name on the list except Pollock’s. She found his address and called on him at his Eighth Street studio. “I was overwhelmed, bowled over, that’s all,” she later said. “I felt as if the floor was sinking when I saw those paintings.” By 1942, they were dating. “Krasner held the more prominent artistic reputation of the two. She was better educated and more firmly entrenched in the close-knit and pugnacious New York art world,” write curators David Breslin and Brinda Kumar in the introduction to the exhibition catalogue. Her paintings of the period “articulated still-life forms and figures in thick paint, fusing geometric shapes with organic forms in overlapping planes over flat backgrounds of white or gray,” with primary blues, reds, and yellows “knit together by strong black lines.” Mondrian was an influence, and she often recalled with pride that he admired these works. Krasner moved into Pollock’s East Eighth Street apartment in fall 1942, and they married in October 1945. A month later, with a $2,000 loan from Peggy Guggenheim, the couple bought a farmhouse and five acres in Springs, complete with a barn. An era of doubt and rebirth The move came in the middle of what Krasner called her “black-out period,” in which, as the catalogue puts it, she built up paint on her canvases but no image emerged, producing her “gray slabs.” Pollock, long in the thrall of Picasso, had finally broken with Cubism, but Krasner wasn’t ready. She said this rupture “took me two years to digest. Between 1943 and 1944 I tried to undo my Cubist orientation and produced very little work in a rather anxious situation.” But her work also took a backseat to Pollock’s career, which she championed using her connections and good graces to earn the truculent Pollock opportunities, introducing him to Robert Motherwell , Roberto Matta , and Surrealist ideas, including automatic drawing. “At the expense of her own work,” art historian Kirk Varnedoe wrote, “Krasner poured her energy and intelligence into furthering Pollock’s efforts.” Scholar Robert Hobbs reads the gray slabs of this era as Krasner grappling with news of the Holocaust, slowly emerging from Europe. Eventually, Krasner broke through this era of artistic doubt. Working in the upstairs bedroom Pollock had vacated, she made the “Little Images,” compact, impastoed canvases of “small dabs of paint intentionally placed in even adjacency” that became “a chromatic prism through which Krasner unlocked an endless palette.” In 1953, following a disappointing solo show in 1951, she began recycling her unsold canvases into large collages. Some of these works include scraps of Pollock’s discarded drawings and canvases, among them Bald Eagle (1955). In the fall of 1955, at the age of 46, Krasner opened a solo exhibition of her collage paintings at dealer Eleanor Ward’s Stable Gallery in New York, marking her second solo show in New York. While dealer Betty Parsons was the show’s only buyer, the exhibition earned strong reviews with Stuart Preston of the New York Times calling her “a good noisy colorist” and Fairfield Porter writing, in ARTnews , that her art “seems to be about nature” and makes viewers “aware of a subtle disorder greater than [they] might otherwise have thought possible.” The show marked a new era of creativity for Krasner. Pollock, in a downward spiral fueled by alcoholism, meanwhile created only one painting that year. Krasner’s crescendo After moving into the barn in 1957, Krasner’s scale and her palette changed. In early 1958, she exhibited 17 of her “Earth Green” paintings, large-scale bright abstractions seemingly inspired by nature, at Martha Jackson Gallery. Stuart Preston wrote in a review in the Times that “the sheer energy that Miss Krasner manages to generate on her picture surfaces.” Her work went well beyond her canvases, however. Krasner worked tirelessly to secure Pollock’s legacy, and became a key source for critics and curators writing about him. She collaborated on the 1958 traveling retrospective of his work and placed his estate with Marlborough Gallery. When Marlborough’s director offered to represent her too, she declined, preferring to be asked on her own terms, not as his executor. After her mother died in 1959, insomnia drove Krasner to paint at night under artificial light. The result was the “Umber” series, which the critic Cindy Nemser described as “slashing, splintered strokes of raw umber and white.” By the mid-1960s, bright colors had returned in works like Combat (year), which measures more than 5 by 13 feet, in riotous twists and folds of pink and orange color. In 1965, Krasner took a step out of Pollock’s shadow when she opened “Lee Krasner: Paintings, Drawings, and Collages,” a retrospective of her work at the Whitechapel Gallery , her first solo exhibition outside the U.S. In 1974, the curator Bryan Robertson found a box of her 1930s drawings from Hofmann’s classes. She cut them into strips and shards, and rebuilt them as canvases named for verb tenses. “I am never free of the past,” she said. “I believe in continuity… the past is part of the present which becomes part of the future.” At the end of her life, Krasner was looking to the future through her own past. The ailing artist donated her assets, made up mainly from her work and Pollock’s, to create a foundation that would support the work of young artists. The Pollock-Krasner Foundation has granted over $90 million to artists since it was established in 1985, and is the first successful foundation established by an artist, for artists.

title: Anina Major’s Giant Woven Ceramic Towers Rethink Bahamian Craft Traditions
summary: Water Tower, 2024 Anina Major TERN Gallery In Anina Major ’s sculpture Water Tower (2024), strips of woven stoneware climb upward into a 45-inch-tall column, its ombré glaze deepening from pale aqua to rich turquoise. Melted sea glass glints across its irregular surface, while sand gathers around its base. The piece exemplifies the artist’s engagement with palm plaiting, a Bahamian weaving tradition that women have passed down for generations, often as a crucial source of their own income. Major expands the woven form, giving a familiar craft language a monumental presence. In 2024, Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM) acquired the sculpture, which will appear in “ The Sacred Mangrove ,” Major’s first solo presentation at a major international institution. The show, organized by curator Jennifer Inacio, will open at PAMM on October 1st. At the museum, Major’s towering ceramic forms rise like sentinels throughout the waterfront gallery. Folkloric bottle trees create a protective presence. Shells and reused ceramic shards scatter across the ground, while a soundscape recorded on a Bahamian beach brings the acoustics of the artist’s home country into the installation. “I was thinking about the similarities between Miami and The Bahamas,” Major told Artsy. “Not just how Miami has functioned within the historical context of Bahamian culture, but this idea of connecting entities, drawing a line between the two.” With her installation, the artist intends to “command more space and prominence,” enhancing the impact she can make as she works at a larger scale. The PAMM exhibition arrives weeks after the opening of “ SOON COME HOME ,” Major’s second solo presentation with TERN Gallery in Nassau, The Bahamas, on view through October 26th. The shows honor an artist who’s nearly a decade into her unique, hybrid practice of translating plaiting into ceramics. Major began experimenting with this process while studying ceramics at the Rhode Island School of Design, where she earned her MFA in 2017. She learned plaiting through her grandmother, Saphora Alvina Timothy Newbold, known as Mar, who passed the tradition on to other women in The Bahamas. Major has since studied how weaving patterns traveled across the islands and changed from place to place, something she describes as “repetition with adaptation.” Major cuts rolled slabs of clay into thin strips, then weaves them while they are still pliable. In “The Sacred Mangrove,” she primarily uses plain weave (a simple over-under pattern that creates a checkerboard appearance), while sculptures including Rooted Sky (2026) and Forgotten Maiden No. 3 (2025) incorporate twill and reed-based patterns. Major often works early in the morning, when ideas come faster than she can realize them. She describes her process as responsive: “There’s something about the clay that tells you when it’s ready to be done,” she said. House in the Sky, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery Skyscraper, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery That extends to glazing. She said she favors a “rich, juicy” surface, with built-up layers. The kiln introduces its own variables, warping the clay or shifting a glaze in ways she cannot fully anticipate. The artist builds further richness through firing techniques and materials beyond clay. In House in the Sky (2026), on view in “SOON COME HOME,” sand and flocking meet a glossy glaze that shifts from mossy green to cream. The Kumbla (2026) pairs salt-fired stoneware with sea glass and sand, its deep blue and violet giving way to areas of pale stoneware. At first, ceramics offered Major a way to preserve the knowledge she had inherited. Her early works drew from woven bags and dolls associated with Bahamian tourism. Major remembers looking at a souvenir small enough to fit in her palm and wondering what would happen if she deconstructed and magnified it. That impulse eventually produced works like Sandcastle (2025), a roughly 1,100-pound stoneware sculpture that grew out of experiments she began during a 2023 residency at the European Ceramic Work Centre. The Kumbla, 2026 Anina Major TERN Gallery In 2025, Major settled in upstate New York, where she began renovating a former service station into a studio with room for her increasingly ambitious work. That year, Sandcastle was named a finalist for the Loewe Foundation Craft Prize . For Major, enlarging these forms is about how the traditions behind them are valued. “I’m not trying to replace souvenirs in the marketplace,” she said. “I’m actually trying to shift perception and value around that work.” As her sculptures grew, Major also began thinking about how her individual pieces could inhabit space together. Seeing Betye Saar ’s show “Serious Moonlight” at ICA Miami in 2021 brought Major to tears. “I felt seen,” she said. “I was moved by how she allows her symbolic vocabulary to expand spatially.” The exhibition showed her how individual sculptures could become part of an immersive, room-sized installation. Major also looked to Japanese American ceramic artist Toshiko Takaezu , whose Homage to Devastation Forest (1982 – 1987), exhibited in the Noguchi Museum ’s 2024 retrospective “Toshiko Takaezu: Worlds Within,” brings ceramic forms together as a sculptural landscape. In “The Sacred Mangrove,” Major pushes her work in this direction, treating the exhibition space as an environment rather than a backdrop for individual sculptures. The mangrove became her framework, connecting Miami and The Bahamas through an ecosystem native to each place. Major describes it as “connective tissue” between them. PAMM’s glass-walled space overlooking Biscayne Bay further shaped the installation, which remains visible from outside after dark. In Nassau, Major’s work is expanding through material. “SOON COME HOME” marks the first time her signature ceramic doll series (including Brassy , 2025), inspired by the straw dolls sold in Bahamian tourist markets, appears in glass. For Major, home remains a source of inspiration and a place to return to as her practice continues to evolve. “There’s this weird thing that feels like this is just the beginning,” she said.

title: Why Mary Cassatt’s Iconic Painting of a Little Girl Is So Radical
summary: “I love to paint children,” Mary Cassatt once said. “They are so natural and truthful. They have no arrière-pensée (ulterior motive).” The American-born Impressionist became one of the most influential artists of 19th-century France with her refreshingly tender portraits of mothers and children painted in loose, tactile brushstrokes. Among her most famous paintings is Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878), now in the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C. The painting shows a young, tired-looking girl slouching in a large floral blue armchair, a small Brussels griffon dog resting in a matching chair nearby. She wears a bored expression, her limbs sprawled over the chair in exhaustion or exasperation. This frank expression captures Cassatt’s modern, secular approach to portraying children. This year marks the centennial of Cassatt’s death in 1926 at age 82. In response, many museums are honoring her life and work. The Musée d’Orsay is opening “Mary Cassatt: Being Independent” (“ Mary Cassatt: L’Indépendante” ) on October 6th, an exhibition of nearly 80 paintings, pastels, and prints. The exhibition will travel to Boston in 2027. Meanwhile, the Art Institute of Chicago is currently hosting “Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism,” which looks at her career in the years after the final Impressionist exhibition of 1886. To mark the centennial of her life, we’ve taken a closer look at Cassatt’s celebrated Little Girl in a Blue Armchair . Cassatt collaborated with Degas to create this iconic work La Petite Danseuse de 14 Ans, 1881 Edgar Degas Théo Landel Cassatt was born in 1844 in Allegheny City, Pennsylvania, to a wealthy American family. Initially, her parents resisted her ambition to become a professional artist, but by 1860, a teenage Cassatt had enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. She moved to Europe in her twenties, eventually settling in Paris, where she would live for the rest of her life. Cassatt’s early works took inspiration from the Old Masters , whom she studied closely on painting trips through Italy, Spain, and the Netherlands. Over the years, however, her brushwork loosened and her palette brightened, and she began experimenting with the asymmetrical compositions and unconventional croppings influenced by the nascent Impressionist art movement and the dawn of photography. By 1877, Cassatt’s works had come into open conflict with the French art establishment and the official Salon rejected both of her submissions that year. That rejection spurred Edgar Degas to invite her to exhibit with the Impressionists, an invitation she accepted. Degas’s friendship with Cassatt shaped Little Girl in a Blue Armchair . The girl in the painting was the daughter of friends of Degas’s, but his contribution extended far beyond that. “It was the portrait of a friend of M. Degas,” Cassatt wrote to the Parisian dealer Ambroise Vollard in 1903. “I had done the child in the armchair and he found it good and advised me on the background and he even worked on it.” Recent cleaning and infrared imaging at the National Gallery of Art have since confirmed his work on the canvas. Scholars believe Degas most likely reworked the oddly shaped patch of floor between the chairs and the play of light through the windows, and his influence has been traced through the painting’s asymmetrical composition, its bold pattern, and its tight, cropped framing—a debt to the Japanese prints he introduced Cassatt to. The little girl enacts a rebellion against adult society The psychology of the painting, however, is quintessentially Cassatt’s. The girl becomes an agent of disorder and rebellion in the tidy adult world she inhabits. Her body sprawls diagonally across the blue-and-white floral chair, cutting against the orderly lines of the upholstery. Her expression sits somewhere between boredom and open irritation, her gaze drifting sideways toward the little dog curled up in the matching armchair beside her. Her look might be one of envy. The dog, unlike her, is unencumbered by expectations. The girl is painted, not in a nursery where she might be at ease, but a fashionable drawing room, the domain of adult women. The girl fidgets under the constraints. Feminist writer Germaine Greer called the painting Cassatt’s “first real stunner,” which she saw “as an icon of the awfulness of being at once controlled by adults and ignored by them.” The composition reinforces this sense of claustrophobia, with chairs pressing in from every side. The girl’s averted gaze here becomes an assertion of her own independence—an autonomy Cassatt celebrates. The painting caused a controversy when it debuted Afternoon Tea Party, 1991 Mary Cassatt Canopy Gallery In the Omnibus, 1991 Mary Cassatt Canopy Gallery Cassatt took an interest in the lives of women and children well beyond the canvas. She was a feminist from an early age and spent her career depicting the “New Woman” of the 19th century. These women went out in society, receiving guests, going to the theater, and conquering the modern world on their own terms. Cassatt was one of these women as well. “I am independent!” she once declared. “I can live alone and I love to work.” Cassatt, unlike many of her era, did not reserve that sense of self-possession for adults. Art historian Griselda Pollock has called Little Girl in a Blue Armchair one of the most “radical” images of childhood because of its lack of sentimentality. But Cassatt’s frank depiction of childhood also put off viewers acclimated to more idealized imagery. She submitted the painting to the American pavilion at the 1878 Paris World’s Fair, and its jury rejected it. The decision infuriated Cassatt, particularly because Degas had worked on it. “I sent it to the American section of the big exposition, they refused it,” she wrote to Vollard. “I was furious, all the more so since he had worked on it. At that time this appeared new and the jury consisted of three people of which one was a pharmacist!” Cassatt never knew what had turned the jury off of the work, but in the nearly 150 years since its creation, Little Girl in a Blue Armchair has earned a much warmer reception. The painting entered the collection of the National Gallery of Art in 1983, and has remained one of the most popular works at the museum since.

title: KAWS collaborates with Absolut Vodka on limited-edition bottle and painting.
summary: KAWS has collaborated with Absolut Vodka on a new Artist Edition bottle. The design is inspired by a painting KAWS created for the project, with Absolut’s apothecary-style bottle featuring his signature “XX” motif and his signature Chum character on the front of the bottle and an image of the original painting on the back. “I am excited to join the lineage of great artists that have worked with Absolut Vodka over the decades,” KAWS said in a statement. “My goal is to allow art to meet people in unexpected places, and I hope my bottles will be enjoyed at gatherings around the world.” KAWS, whose real name is Brian Donnelly, is known for his cartoon-like figures and artworks that sit at the intersection of street culture, fine art, and commercial goods. His works have been shown at institutions including the Brooklyn Museum , the Serpentine Gallery , and the Albertina Modern in Vienna. The Absolut partnership follows a string of brand collaborations for the artist, including a 2025 appointment as UNIQLO's first artist in residence and, this past June, a redesign of the packaging for Austria's Sacher-Torte to benefit a children’s charity. The collaboration extends Absolut’s decades-long history of working with artists on its bottle. Andy Warhol painted “Absolut Warhol” in 1985, becoming the brand’s first artist-designed advertisement and prompting Warhol to recommend Keith Haring as a successor collaborator. Since the 1980s, more than 550 artists have contributed over 850 artworks inspired by the bottle, a collection now housed at Stockholm’s Spritmuseum. “Our collaboration with KAWS reimagines the iconic Absolut bottle as a witty, unexpected work of art that feels at home on a collector’s shelf or at the center of a gathering with friends,” said Caroline Begley, Absolut’s U.S. vice president of marketing, in a statement. “By bringing KAWS’ remarkable vision to one of our most iconic assets, we’re creating a cultural statement piece that celebrates creativity, self-expression and the power of art to connect people.” The Absolut KAWS Artist Edition bottle is available for pre-order at Absolut.com and will roll out to select U.S. retailers for a limited time while supplies last.

title: Chiharu Shiota’s Monumental Thread Installations Hold a Lifetime of Memories
summary: How many memories can the length of thread hold? In Chiharu Shiota ’s hands, the answer seems boundless. For the Japanese artist, thread can evoke feelings of fear and uncertainty, as well as resilience and strength. Shiota’s immersive installations in black, white, or red thread are like intricate webs that visitors can walk through, and they often include found objects like shoes, dresses, or suitcases. “When I’m weaving, it’s like meditation,” Shiota told Artsy. “For hours, I follow the same pattern, and all my feelings go into this process. If I’m anxious or my feelings are more mixed up, then you can see it in the thread.” Born in Japan in 1972 and based in Berlin, Shiota has been making thread installations for decades. Her work has earned her international renown, including major exhibitions worldwide and, in 2015, the artist represented Japan at the Venice Biennale. In “Chiharu Shiota: The Soul Trembles,” the artist’s survey at the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts (MMFA), which opened September 26th, Shiota’s evolution from painter to performer to thread-based installation artist is on full view. Today, it’s a moment of self-reflection during an illustrious career that has seen her overcoming dire health challenges. Chiharu Shiota’s early career When she began studying art in the early 1990s, however, Shiota had other disciplines in mind. “I always wanted to be a painter,” she explained, “but while studying I couldn’t paint anymore, the paint had no feeling, I had no identity with paint.” Shiota soon began exploring other media and, in 1994, she staged Becoming Painting , a performance at the Australian National University School of Art in Canberra. At the time, she had a dream that she had become a painting. For the performance, she covered herself with canvas and red enamel paint. She saw this as an “act of liberation,” she recalled. “This was the first artwork that was not a refined, polished art piece, but rather an active bodily expression that I had thrown my entire self into.” In 1996, Shiota moved to Berlin and began studying under Marina Abramović , which was actually a mix-up. Shiota thought she was going to work with fiber artist Magdalena Abakanowicz . However, as Shiota explored performance further, she became interested in creating art without the body. It was this concern that drew her to incorporate objects to stand for human presence, like suitcases, dresses, and shoes often associated with her work today. “I only work with objects that have been used and therefore have memory inside, for example I have collected old suitcases because I can see a person in each suitcase,” she said. “There is a feeling of someone present even though no one is there.” By the late 1990s, Shiota began to shift her focus to using thread as a medium. “When I started using thread, it was like I was drawing in the air,” she said. “I could put all my energy into it.” Confronting her mortality through thread The Montreal exhibition is the first North American presentation of “The Soul Trembles,” which has traveled extensively worldwide since premiering at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum in 2019. The MMFA is the 10th venue to host the show. Spanning more than three decades of Shiota’s career, the exhibition unfolds chronologically and includes monumental installations alongside sculpture, drawings, videos, photographs of her performances, and material related to her work in theater. Planning for the exhibition began around the same time Shiota received her second cancer diagnosis in 2017. While thinking about her body, she struggled to understand where her soul fit within the tumultuous process of healing. These concerns permeate her work. In Out of My Body (2019), red leather cut to resemble a net is suspended in the air, hanging like torn skin. On the floor beneath sit bronze casts of the artist’s limbs. The piece responds directly to Shiota’s emotional state as she grappled with cancer. “She’s had moments when she’s had to face her mortality,” said Iris Amizlev, MMFA curator of special projects. “The work resembles Shiota’s body torn apart, as if she was on an assembly line. The diagnosis and healing became like a mechanical process, and she suffered terribly.” Though the survey show has been traveling for years, Shiota rebuilds the thread installations in each institution. “Every time I work with the new space, I must imagine how the artwork will change, could it become wider, smaller, or higher,” she said. “I have to visit the exhibition space before I can decide how to create it anew. Everything depends on the space.” The installations are built from countless small gestures. At the MMFA, the process took roughly three weeks with dozens of people working, including those from Shiota’s studio and students from Montreal’s Concordia University. As the installation takes shape, threads cross, knot, and stretch across the gallery. “Black thread is like a pencil line, an accumulation of black lines creates something more abstract like the night sky or the universe, red represents blood and connection, white is used for funerals in Japan; it presents an end but also a new beginning,” the artist said. Themes of connection in Shiota’s work In the installation In Silence (2002/2026), black thread fills the room, casting a dark shadow across the dimly lit space. A seemingly charred piano and chairs sit within the dense thread matrix. The work is based on a childhood memory from when Shiota was nine. At the time, her neighbor’s house caught fire and a scorched piano was left outside. While it no longer functioned, the artist recalled, she felt its beauty radiate even more than before the fire. In Uncertain Journey (2016/2026), a dense matrix of red thread flows through the large gallery. “Visitors walk through and under the installation, activating the work with their presence,” Amizlev said. Connected to the thread are several large metal boats, an object Shiota uses often to represent immigration, displacement, and the broader journey of life. “While boats can be used as guides, we all face an uncertain future together and as individuals,” Amizlev added. “These existential moments unite us across borders and cultures—it’s one of the reasons why Shiota’s work is so universally relevant.” As “The Soul Trembles” travels, the show offers Shiota a prolonged look back at her career and the themes that seem to persist. “[My practice] has always been about memory and the existence in the absence,” she said. “An empty room can still have presence. Someone wa s living there before; I can feel them even though I have never met them.” While addressing these themes, as well as myriad conditions of life that unite us as humans, Shiota leaves her work open to personal connections and interpretations. “Everyone thinks and feels differently,” she said. “Art touches people’s hearts. It’s important that we can share these feelings, inspire each other, and relate to one another.”

title: MacArthur “Genius Grant” 2026 winners include Christine Sun Kim and Rodney McMillian.
summary: The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation has announced the recipients of its 2026 MacArthur Fellowship. Among the 20 recipients of the annual “genius grant” are visual artists Christine Sun Kim , based in Berlin, Rodney McMillian , of Los Angeles, Vincent Valdez , who splits time between Houston and San Antonio, and Chip Thomas, of Flagstaff, Arizona. Each awardee receives an $800,000 no-strings stipend, dispersed over five years. “For 45 years, MacArthur Fellows have defied boundaries by questioning conventions, crossing disciplines, and driving collective progress,” said Kristen Mack, the foundation’s vice president for communications, MacArthur Fellows, and partnerships, in a statement. “The 2026 Fellows continue that creative tradition—they explore the depths of our humanity; they reveal untold origins to modern challenges; they expand the edges of scientific inquiry and life-saving research. They show us new ways to understand the world.” Kim’s work draws attention to ableism as it relates to Deafness. She was recently the subject of a survey at the Whitney Museum of American Art and is known for series like “Degrees of Deaf Rage” (2018–19), drawings recounting moments when hearing privilege collides with Deaf life. She memorably performed the national anthem in American Sign Language at the 2020 Super Bowl. “I am an artist illuminating cultural dimensions of sound and hearing,” she said in her MacArthur announcement video. Kim, who has two children, told the New York Times the funding would let her “scale back on taking opportunities” and “be a little bit more of a mom with more flexibility in her life.” McMillian works across painting, sculpture, video, performance, and installation to examine how history, socioeconomic conditions, and public policy shape quality of life, particularly for Black Americans in the U.S. South. His works range from the 88-foot abstract painting In This Land (2019) to From Asterisks in Dockery (2012), inspired by a chapel once on Mississippi's Dockery Plantation. Valde works primarily as a painter, examining racism and the Latinx experience in the U.S. Major works include the expressionist Kill the Pachuco Bastard! (2001) to the hyperrealist, 30-foot The Beginning Is Near, An American Trilogy, Ch. 1: The City (2016), depicting hooded Klan members. Valdez’s work was the subject of a traveling survey “Just a Dream…” in 2024–25. Thomas worked as a physician on the Navajo Nation for 36 years. The artist makes large-scale public photo murals often installed in abandoned buildings across the reservation, and founded the Painted Desert Project, bringing graffiti artists to make new work there. The rest of this year's class spans economics, physics, chemistry, choreography, and literature, and includes poet Layli Long Soldier, a citizen of the Oglala Lakota Nation whose 2017 poem “He Sápa” lent its title to Jeffrey Gibson 's 2024 U.S. Pavilion presentation at the Venice Biennale.

title: 8 Contemporary Artists Inspired By René Magritte
summary: The work of René Magritte needs little introduction. Since his death in 1967, he has become one of the defining painters of the 20th century, his work influencing generations of artists while also permeating the world of popular culture at almost every level. Referenced by everyone from The Beatles to The Simpsons, his visual vocabulary—bowler-hatted men, veiled faces, enormous apples, and levitating rocks—has left a profound mark on the worlds of advertising, graphic design, film, and photography. No other artist fused the ordinary with the uncanny so seamlessly, or shifted so effortlessly between a sense of ambiguity, dread, and deadpan humor tinged with occasional vulgarity. His enigmatic paintings, such as The Treachery of Images (1929) or The Human Condition (1933), transform everyday objects, places, and figures into surreal , psychologically charged puzzles. Combining an almost hyperrealist style with jarring shifts of scale, trompe l’oeil illusions, and visual fragmentation, his works raise fundamental questions about the boundaries between reality and representation. Now, a major new exhibition at Gagosian in London seeks to trace his enduring legacy on the art world. “This is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte” (through December 12) brings together dozens of the artist’s key paintings and works on paper, setting them in dialogue with work by almost 50 contemporary artists. As Jasper Sharp, the show’s co-curator, explained to Artsy, Magritte’s influence is by no means a recent phenomenon. “You have artists who were already making work in the ’50s thinking about Magritte, so his influence was already taking shape while he was still alive.” But the idea for the current show evolved when it became clear how great a shadow his work still casts in the 21st century. “Over the past few years, I've found myself having so many conversations about Magritte, unprompted by myself, with painters, filmmakers, and photographers.” For Sharp, the explanation for this is twofold. “I think the reason that his works have such an enduring appeal is that they disclose themselves very quickly. But, like all really interesting art, they also work on a different level. They’re not completely understandable.” At the same time, his work is technically masterful, another source of inspiration for artists. As Sharp pointed ut, “ Max Ernst famously described Magritte as a collagist in paint. Which is why he’s been so influential in the graphic design industry, the music industry, and the fashion industry. The way his works are constructed with different surfaces, different depths, gives so much potential to people who want to take his ideas and run with them.” With this in mind, here are eight contemporary artists who share some affinity with Magritte’s themes and approach. The first four are featured in the Gagosian show, while the others are our own recommendations. Lenz Geerk B. 1988, Basel. Lives and works in Düsseldorf. Man holding the night sky, 2024 Lenz Geerk Roberts Projects With their muted palettes and enigmatic subject matter, the paintings of Lenz Geerk exude a strong sense of Magrittean disquiet. Like the Belgian master, his work is steeped in art history, and the figures, objects, and places he depicts seem deeply rooted in the world of dreams. In Tie III (2024), a man in a suit stands stiffly against a bare wall, gazing at his tie unfurled on the floor at his feet, while in Man Holding the Night Sky (2024), a figure stands atop a rock, unfurling a black sheet emblazoned with stars. Cryptic and mysterious, Geerk’s work carefully balances what to reveal and what to withhold. Dominique Fung B. 1987, Ottawa, Canada. Lives and works in Brooklyn, New York. Look Steadily and Intently, 2021 Dominique Fung Woaw Born in Canada, but with ancestry in Shanghai and Hong Kong, Dominique Fung ’s work is inspired by Asian artefacts encountered in museums during her youth. Reimagined through a contemporary lens, she liberates these objects from their colonial or imperialist histories, imbuing them with a new and complex life of their own. Blending older traditions of European painting—whether Baroque , Rococo , or Renaissance —with a Surrealist streak recalling Magritte and Dorothea Tanning , works such as Stray Hair (2020) and Look Steadily and Intently (2021) have a dreamlike quality that hints at unsettling narratives just beyond our grasp. And, much like Magritte, her works operate on multiple levels. Combining elements of humor and the uncanny, their sensuous and exquisitely painted surfaces conceal more serious undertones lurking beneath. Joseph Yaeger B. 1986, Helena, Montana. Lives and works in London. Joseph Yaeger’s paintings, like Magritte’s, are full of secrets. Opaque, voyeuristic, and enigmatically titled, they are charged with a noirish atmosphere of mystery and uncertainty, occupying an uneasy space somewhere between dreams and cinema stills (on which many of them are based). The faces of his figures are often veiled or obscured—by smoke, shadows, bandages, or another person’s hand—resisting any straightforward emotional or psychological interpretation. In particular, they recall iconic works by Magritte, such as The Lovers (1928) or The Son of Man (1946). Working in watercolor on gesso, his works combine technical mastery with subtle hints of decay, their scarred and cracked surfaces dusted with studio debris, evoking a pervasive sense of dread or unease that underpins so many aspects of modern existence. New works by Yaeger will go on view at Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo later this fall. Isabelle Albuquerque B. 1981, Los Angeles. Lives and works in Los Angeles. Call Me, 2024 Isabelle Albuquerque Newchild Gallery Just as Magritte would sometimes depict the human form in fragmented, transfigured, or impossible states (as in Le Viol (1934/1945), in which a naked female torso merges with a woman’s face), Isabelle Albuquerque deconstructs the physical form to create formally complex sculptures with strong echoes of the surreal. Exploring women’s experience of desire, sexuality, and violence, she combines traditional techniques with contemporary technologies like 3D scans and lifecasts of her own body to create headless, truncated, or otherwise transmuted figures. Often merging biological forms with manufactured, mundane, or mythological elements, her sculptures serve as prime examples of the ‘surreal object’, inviting any number of readings and interpretations. In the Gagosian show, her work Summertime Sadness (2024), in which a shock of fire-red human hair sprouts from a bronze cast of a dismembered arm, has definite affinities with Magritte. As Sharp pointed out, it was “the first object she suggested when we approached her for the exhibition.” Kate Meissner B. 1995, Sacramento. Lives and works in Los Angeles. Kate Meissner ’s highly saturated, theatrically lit oil paintings present a mysterious shadow world in which familiar scenes are made alluringly strange. The female figures she depicts are elusive, possessed of an eerie, plastic quality somewhere between human and mannequin. Their faces are always obscured, their bodies contorted and partially veiled by fabric, and their limbs either prosthetic or missing altogether. Often framed in tightly enclosed spaces such as doorways, nightclub booths, or peep-show stages, their compressed, claustrophobic settings evoke a palpable sense of unease while also hinting at unconscious or hidden desires. Blending the surrealism of Magritte with the body horror of filmmaker David Cronenberg , Meissner’s work fearlessly explores the complex emotional and psychological consequences for women of being on display, creating a potent cocktail of apprehension, dread, and curiosity. Natalia Gonzalez Martin B. 1995, Madrid. Lives and works in London. Cascara II , 2024 Natalia Gonzalez Martin Richard Saltoun Painted on wood panels using egg tempera and rabbit skin glue, the exquisitely detailed paintings of Natalia Gonzalez Martin hark back to medieval icons, Renaissance altarpieces, and illuminated manuscripts. However, the atmosphere she creates within these confined spaces remains compellingly odd, infused with a healthy dose of Magrittean Surrealism, ambiguity, and eroticism. Filtered through the lens of her Catholic upbringing, Gonzalez Martin renders everyday objects strange, poetic, or mystical. She often isolates body parts or objects, placing them in flat, shadowless voids, disrupting the viewer’s sense of reality. And, while her paintings sometimes hint at religious ritual and symbolism, their meaning is much more opaque, evoking both past and present, divine and secular, suggesting that there are other ways to exist within the world. Zhou Song B. 1982, Jiangxi, China. Lives and works in Beijing. Wisdom Tree I, 2025 Zhou Song Maddox Gallery Holy Light, 2024 Zhou Song Volery Gallery A mind-bending mixture of hyperrealism and surreal flights of fancy, Zhou Song’s remarkable oil paintings explore both the anxieties and the sense of possibility engendered by an age of constant technological acceleration. In his work, natural and artificial elements are distorted and reconfigured in uncanny new forms as the world we know unravels before our eyes. In Wisdom Tree I (2025), for instance, pencils coil through trees like branches, while in other works, candles twist together like snakes, and a rabbit balances a tower of hats on its back. His “New Nature” series (2020–26) is like Magritte reimagined for the post-human age, and borrows freely from the Belgian artist’s iconic repertoire of motifs. Men in suits, apples, bowler hats, and blue skies full of clouds all feature prominently. Indeed, Homeland (2020) is a direct homage to Magritte’s famous painting The Great War (1964). Kristen Sanders B. 1989, California. Lives and works in St. Paul, Minnesota. Shell/Tool, 2023 Kristen Sanders Asya Geisberg Gallery Hand and Flint, 2023 Kristen Sanders Moosey Magritte’s work often explored the gulf between the physical body and the consciousness within it, and the vividly colored paintings of Kristen Sanders operate in a similar psychological space, reframing it for an era in which artificial intelligence is quickly becoming a reality. The world she conjures is one of mystery and uncertainty—a kind of fever dream in which past and future, human and mechanical, have merged, and the viewer is never sure exactly what they are seeing. A sense of Magrittean surrealism pervades her work. In Stone/Shift (2023), the face of a humanoid robot is obscured by a piece of sheer silk, while in Body Thing (2023) a hand holds a fragment of a human face, its single eye staring helplessly out at the viewer. And A Sense of Reality (2023), in which a piece of flint hovers in mid air against a cloudy sky, makes a direct reference to Magritte’s The Castle of the Pyrenees (1959).

title: Louis Vuitton launches Keith Haring handbag collection.
summary: Louis Vuitton has unveiled the eighth chapter of its Artycapucines collection, dedicating 13 new bag designs to the work of Keith Haring . Developed in collaboration with the Keith Haring Foundation, the collection features the late artist’s vibrant visual language—including his signature “Running Heart,” “ Radiant Baby ,” dancing figures, and exuberant graphic compositions. These motifs are translated into designs using different craft techniques, from traditional leather marquetry to cutting-edge laser printing. Haring, who was born in Pennsylvania in 1958 and died in 1990, became one of the defining voices of New York’s downtown art scene in the 1980s, creating graphic works that moved fluidly between street art , gallery walls, and broader culture. His work, characterized by bold outlines, rhythmic figures, and a sense of collective joy, is some of the most recognizable in post-war American art. Beyond the art world, Haring’s imagery has retained a broad cultural presence. His figures have appeared on everything from UNIQLO T-shirts to stadium murals, and his work continues to be cited by a generation of artists, designers, and musicians. The new designs continue the collaboration between the Keith Haring Foundation and the French fashion house. Earlier this year, Louis Vuitton presented clothing printed with Haring’s designs at its womenswear presentation at New York’s Frick Collection . Highlights of the new 13-piece collection include the Capucines Nano Running Heart, a minaudière , or vanity case , crafted in silver-tone metal and set with more than 12,000 hand-placed rhinestones; and the Capucines MM Genesis, inspired by a Louis Vuitton suitcase hand-customised by Haring in 1984. The Capucines East-West Mini Maze, is brought to life through intricate bead embroidery, and the Capucines BB Figures feature Haring’s dancing figures on pristine white Taurillon leather, his characteristic black outline integrated into the bag’s architecture. Louis Vuitton’s Artycapucines Collection, which launched in 2019, now comprises more than 50 designs by artists including Takashi Murakami , Tschabalala Self , Urs Fischer , and Park Seo-Bo . All 13 pieces from the Haring edition will be released as limited editions in Louis Vuitton stores worldwide from January 1, 2027.
